intro: This is the second movement of Tchaikovsky’s Piano Concerto No. 1 in B♭ minor, Op. 23, in D♭ major; the flute plays the theme over plucked strings, and the piano follows. The fast central section is built on a French song that Tchaikovsky’s brothers used to sing.

sections.label: A · Flute melody, pizzicato strings, D♭ major
sections.mNote: The D♭-major melody passes from flute to piano.

sections.label: B · Prestissimo, piano and French song
sections.mNote: The Prestissimo begins in F major.

sections.label: A′ · Opening melody returns, piano
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns with new decoration in the piano.

sections.label: Coda · D♭ major, final cadence
sections.mNote: The oboe completes the tune before the final cadence.

cues.title: Flute and plucked strings
cues.text: Over pizzicato strings, the flute plays the D♭-major melody in bars 5–12. The piano takes over the tune in bars 13–20.
cues.evidence: Second-movement opening and solo handover: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky). Tonic Chord identifies flute bars 5–12 and piano bars 13–20: https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two-piano arrangement, January 1875
cues.text: Tchaikovsky had completed the concerto’s two-piano arrangement by 2 January 1875. Three days later he played the work to Nikolay Rubinstein and Nikolay Hubert. He finished the orchestration on 21 February.
cues.evidence: Manuscript date 21 December 1874/2 January 1875; private play-through 24 December/5 January; orchestration completed 9/21 February. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Prestissimo middle section
cues.text: The Prestissimo, a short scherzo in the middle of the slow movement, opens in F major with fast piano writing. The strings then take up a new tune in D major. The piano accompanies them.
cues.evidence: Second-movement middle section, keys and scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky); formal outline at https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: French song in the fast middle section
cues.text: The fast middle section borrows Il faut s’amuser, danser et rire (“one must have fun, dance and laugh”), a tune by Jean-Baptiste-Edouard Montaubry. Modest Tchaikovsky recalled singing it constantly with his brother Anatoly in the early 1870s. Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky put the refrain into his Piano Concerto No. 1.
cues.evidence: Modest Tchaikovsky, The Life of Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, vol. 1 (1900), p. 466, quoted under Related Works. The tune is by Jean-Baptiste-Edouard Montaubry. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Reprise of the opening melody
cues.text: After the fast dance, the opening melody returns in D♭ major. The piano plays it with small ornaments, and the oboe continues it.
cues.evidence: Second-movement reprise: ornamented piano theme followed by oboe, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda in D♭ major
cues.text: The coda is in D♭ major. Its last cadence is plagal, moving from G♭ major to D♭, and is marked ppp.
cues.evidence: The second movement ends ppp with a plagal cadence in D♭ major. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From Andantino to Prestissimo in F major
transitions.from: A · Flute melody, pizzicato strings, D♭ major
transitions.to: B · Prestissimo, piano and French song
transitions.how: At the end of the Andantino the piano holds a high F-major chord, pianissimo. The Prestissimo begins in the same key with fast solo writing for the piano. The strings then play the French song in D major, and the piano accompanies them.
transitions.evidence: High F-major chord, Prestissimo opening and D-major string tune: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: The piano returns to D♭
transitions.from: B · Prestissimo, piano and French song
transitions.how: A cadenza-like piano passage in bars 135–145 ends the fast episode. At bar 146 the soloist plays the opening D♭-major melody again at the slower tempo and adds ornaments to the line the flute played at the start.
transitions.evidence: Tonic Chord identifies the solo link in bars 135–145 and the D♭-major return at bar 146. https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/

transitions.title: Oboe continuation and plagal close
transitions.how: The oboe continues the returning melody and resolves it in D♭ major. A brief coda follows and ends on a G♭-major chord moving to D♭, marked ppp.
transitions.evidence: Oboe continuation, tonic resolution and plagal close: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

composer.epithet: Composer who could write a brilliant ballroom scene and, within it, a single unguarded melody showing that someone present was unhappy.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas came to him in the middle of conversations, and he kept them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper to hand. He held that waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. He then stopped for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, and went on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while giving more and more of his time to opera and concerts.
